Press Release:


Boko Haram Horror
There are reports that Boko Haram has killed at least hundreds if not thousands of people in Northern Nigeria. Carte Blanche explores the growing power of this menacing terrorist group.


Script:


Script

Promo 1: 10”

VO: 6”
Estimates of 2000 dead in Boko Haram’s most deadly insurgency yet in the Nigerian town of Baga.

JJ:
21:35 Jesuis Charlie why not Jesuis Baga?


Promo 2:

VO: 6”
Harrowing accounts of killing sprees committed by extremist Islamic group Boko Haram in Northern Nigeria.

Martin:
18:10…killed like insects…they don’t look human.


Promo 3:

VO: 9”
Nigerian President Goodluck Johnathan sent a message of condolence to French president Francois Hollande…by contrast he’s done little to condemn the killing in his own backyard.

JJ…
It will cost him


SCRIPT

VO: 25
On the 3rd of January Islamic militants belonging to extremist group Boko Haram stormed the town of Baga on the shores of Lake Chad in North Eastern Nigeria. Local officials fear as many as 2000 dead. Satellite images released by Amnesty international this week show devastation of catastrophic proportions. The red dots indicate healthy vegetation – 5 days later sections of the town and nearly 4000 buildings are destroyed. Noel Kututwa is Amnesty’s representative here in South Africa.

Noel:
The effect has terrorized ordinary Nigerians. What Boko Haram does is they target ordinary women and children. They go to villages, they go to towns and they kill indiscriminately.

VO: 4”
More than 16 surrounding villages fell prey to the group.

Noel:
We don’t know how many have been displaced in Nigeria, so we don’t have a number to say Boko Haram are responsible for we don’t know how many actually make it across Lake Chad and how many actually perish as a result of doing that.

Vo: 6”
Heavily armed they have dealt a devastating blow says Africa analyst and broadcaster Jean-Jacques Cornish.

JJ:
Because they are well financed they have high tech military equipment, assault rifles, rocket launchers, that are called the technicals, vehicles carrying heavy machine guns and so the people have no means indeed the army has no means of countering them.

VO: 6”
Brutality is the hallmark of the attacks says counter terrorism expert Martin Ewi.

Martin:
People are killed liked insects, if you look at the killing machine of Boko Haram they don’t look human. Which means they will use very blunt things to kill you,they will use knives to slit your neck, they will cut off your ears, take out your body part so its very, very gruesome.

VO: 4”
Recently the terror group started using young girls as part of their arsenal.

Children used collateral damage – left how many dead VO: 5”
2 separate suicide bombings in busy markets in Borno and Yobe states added a further 31 dead in an ominous escalation of violence last weekend.

JJ:
We have the gruesome description from a bystander on the weekend where they saw the plaited heads of the little girls and the upper torso’s, realizing that they were young girls, preteen girls.

Martin:
These are not suicide bombers these are homicide bombers because these young children are being forced into carrying these bombs and going to explode themselves.

VO: 6”
On Christmas eve a young girl escaped and shared a rare insight into Boko Haram’s heinous schemes.

Zahara U’Adamu
My father took us to the bush which was surrounded by gunmen, I was asked if I wanted to go to heaven. When I answered they said I should go for a suicide mission and if I attempted to run they would kill me. So from there we were sent to Kano. When we arrived there one of us said we should go separately but I refused. Then after my friend detonated her own explosive vest I was wounded.


VO: 18”
For the past 5 years Boko Haram has intensified its assault on communities in the North East of the country. Suicide bombings have left hundreds dead and severely maimed.

Martin:
The purpose is to inflict that fear so that people should obey.

VO:
Then in April last year the world woke up to the kidnapping of nearly 300 schoolgirls in Chibok – and that’s when the organization gained notoriety.

Upsound
I repeat, I took the girls and I will sell them off.

Noel:
World leaders rallied around that issue and there was a lot of lobbying and campaigning to free the girls who were abducted, but what did not follow through was the Nigerian authorities themselves taking up that campaign and owning it.

VO: 4”
But in the absence of decisive action their reign of terror has no boundaries.

Martin:
Pregnant women have been exposed, taken out their children and killed them in front of them.

Different incarnations been around 15 years VO: 7”
These dehumanizing acts are a far cry from Boko Haram’s foundations says Afro Middle East researcher Na’eem Jeenah.

Na’eem:
These organisation’s often start because they are able to tap into legitimate grievances and in the case of Boko Haram a feeling whether real or perceived of marginalization by the centre.

VO: 6”
It’s alleged seed funding came from Osama Bin Laden’s Al Quaeda, but these days Boko Haram are largely funded from inside Nigeria. Their aim to carve out an Islamic state or what’s known as a caliphate.

JJ:
They want to run the country. Boko haram translates as Western education is evil, that’s what Boko Haram means. And as a result of that they want to get rid of everything that is not purely Islamic in the North of Nigeria.

VO: 4”
But drill down and it’s unclear what they really want.

Na’eem:
They have some notion of what they think a state was under the prophet Mohammed 1400 years ago but on details would there be separation of powers between the judiciary and the legislature, many of them are not able to answer that question.

Bongani:
So in the end this is just rhetoric?

Na’eem:
It’s just rhetoric and its playing into a kind of emotion of Muslims who feel we need an Islamic state, we need an Islamic leadership the and groups like ISIS and Boko Haram play into that.

VO: 5”
And it’s for strategic reasons that the town of Baga has become a target.

Map again Martin:
Baga is a strategic city for Boko Haram, it is a strategic city for the government because it is a border city, it provides access to the 4 countries in the Lake Chad basin: Niger, Chad and Cameroon. Boko Haram can easily flee into one of these countries. And it’s a city that is very strategic for supplies.

Bongani link:
President Goodluck Jonathan presides over the larges economy in Africa with a powerful army, yet has been unable to stem the growth of Boko Haram. In the aftermath of the Paris attacks he sent a message of condolence but has hardly uttered a word about what happened in Baga.

JJ:
Goodluck Jonathan who is on the stump for elections on Valentines day next month has not yet said anything about this massacre and the three suicide bombs by young girls. And he’s on the stump. The fact is if he doesn’t do something about this then his opponent, Muhammadu Buhari, who is a military man will say well I will do something, and that will cost him.

VO:
What President Jonathan has said is how traumatised he is by the internal displacement of the victims of the massacre. And while the people of Paris marched on the streets in throngs…there’s been little civil action in Nigeria.

Jj:
You wouldn’t be able to have that there, you don’t have that degree of political sophistication and civil liberty in Nigeria. The authorities would be too fearful of such a thing happening.

VO: 7”
At a summit in France in May last year - President Goodluck Jonathan made promises but could offer little by way of progress.

Goodluck Johnathan:
We’ve been scanning the area with surveillance aircraft and of course also using local intelligence sources, this is being complimented now by France, Uk and other countries.

VO:2”
Now it just seems like more lip service.

Noel:
Accountability, following through and making sure that those commitments that are being made are in fact followed through and those commitments we see results.


VO: 8”
While the politicians fail to deliver the humanitarian crisis mounts says UNICEF Nigeria Emergency Manager Dominic Stolarow.

Dominic:
Over the period of time in 2014 in the three states of emergency over 338 schools were destroyed.

VO: 5”
250000 children are reportedly malnourished and emotionally scarred.

Dominic:
We’ve also set up a psycho social support programme reaching over 12000 children.


VO: 10”
In stark contrast to the intense global media coverage of events in Paris last week – critics are asking why the massacre in Baga isn’t garnering more traction?
Bongani link:
The media has come in for some criticism over its coverage of these latest attacks with some saying that the interest in Paris was disproportionate when you consider the numbers that were killed in Baga. But is it that simple?

JJ:
Jesuis Charlie, why not Jesuis Baga? And that is a legitimate question, the fact is if you see how the integrists or the terrorists were pursued in Paris, I am sure to the chagrin of the security forces, it couldn’t have made their jobs easy, but as television crews were chasing them along with police. That hasn’t happened in Boko Haram, people don’t really know what has happened.

VO: 9”
Inaccessible and dangerous – it’s more than just a case of Western indifference. Even in Nigeria reporting is scant.

AU Visuals VO: 4”
The true elephant in the room, of course is the African Union.

Bongani:
Where is the AU on all of this?

Martin:
Very good question. Where is the African Union in this – the African union are nowhere.

VO: 10”
On Monday this week AU chair Nksosazana Dlamini Zuma issued a statement condemning the acts and offering sympathy but she’s done nothing concrete to mobilise a solution.

Noel:
This mantra of African solutions for African problems and as a result of that African leaders don’t want to hold each other to account. How can you expect one leader to hold the other to account when that very leader has his own skeletonsthat they don’t want to bring out.

Link:
The abducted girls from last year are still missing and with each attack Boko Haram seems to be getting bolder and more violent, with good reason. There is no sense yet that this matter is anywhere closer to a solution so the question is where will it all end?

10’20” Martin:
The massacre is going to continue until we are able to build that collective security, until African leaders , African people are conscious of what is happening elsewhere.
